name: Small Omphalocele

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Imaging Diagnosis of Omphalocele

criteria.description: Presence of a midline abdominal wall defect at the base of the umbilical cord covered by a membranous sac
Defect size less than 5 cm in diameter
Prenatal or postnatal ultrasound or MRI confirming herniation of abdominal contents within a sac
No associated large structural anomalies or chromosomal abnormalities

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of a small midline abdominal wall defect covered by a membranous sac confirmed by imaging
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical and imaging-based; genetic testing may be performed to exclude syndromic associations.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Small midline abdominal wall defect covered by a membranous sac
pathognomonic.notes: Typically located at the base of the umbilical cord
searchTerms: small belly wall gap covered by thin skin

pathognomonic.symptomName: Herniation of abdominal viscera into the sac
searchTerms: internal organs protruding through abdominal defect

common.symptomName: Umbilical cord insertion at the edge of the defect
searchTerms: umbilical cord attached at edge of defect
cord insertion at abdominal wall opening

common.symptomName: Thin translucent sac covering the herniated contents
common.notes: Sac consists of peritoneum and amnion
Due to abdominal wall defect and associated visceral displacement
searchTerms: poor sucking or swallowing in neonates

occasional.symptomName: Delayed closure of the abdominal wall defect
searchTerms: slow healing of abdominal wall opening

occasional.notes: May coexist or develop post repair

rare.notes: More common in larger omphaloceles but rare in small
May occur if sac ruptures or is exposed

laboratory: Normal routine blood tests unless complications occur
Blood cultures if sac infection suspected
imaging: Prenatal ultrasound showing anterior abdominal wall defect with herniated viscera
Postnatal abdominal ultrasound or MRI confirming sac and contents
genetic: Karyotyping to exclude chromosomal abnormalities if syndromic features present
other: Physical examination revealing characteristic sac and defect
Surgical findings confirming defect size and contents

distinguishingFeatures: No covering sac over herniated viscera
Often associated with other congenital anomalies
May include liver herniation more frequently

redFlags: Rupture or infection of the omphalocele sac
Respiratory distress due to compromised diaphragmatic function
references: Moore KL, Persaud TVN. The Developing Human: Clinically Oriented Embryology. 11th Edition. 2015.
Sadler TW. Langman’s Medical Embryology. 14th Edition. 2019.
